title: Review an API that retries every exception indefinitely
description: Problem: Review an API that retries every exception indefinitely. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: An API endpoint wraps all outgoing calls in an unconditional retry loop. When a downstream service returns a 400 Bad Request or a 401 Unauthorized, the client retries immediately and forever. The downstream service is hammered with redundant requests, its error logs fill with stack traces, and the client thread is blocked indefinitely. Under partial failure, this pattern turns a small outage into a cascading failure that brings down both services.

items: Understand the difference between retryable and non-retryable HTTP status codes
Learn exponential backoff and jitter as defenses against thundering herds
Identify circuit breaker patterns that stop retries when a downstream is clearly failing
Apply Polly or System.Threading.RateLimiting to implement bounded, policy-driven retries

terms.definition: Repeating a failed operation in the hope that it will succeed on a subsequent attempt.
Increasing the wait time between retries exponentially to reduce load on a struggling downstream.
Adding randomness to retry delays to prevent synchronized retries from many clients at once.
A pattern that stops retries after a threshold of failures, allowing the downstream to recover.

data.text: Indefinite retries are the most common cause of cascading failures in distributed systems. A client that retries every exception without limit or delay turns a 500 error into a denial of service against the downstream. The downstream, already struggling, receives even more traffic, returns more errors, and triggers more retries. The loop continues until either the client runs out of threads or the downstream recovers on its own, which it cannot do under sustained load.

data.title: Not all errors are retryable
data.text: A 400 Bad Request means the client sent invalid data. Retrying it will never succeed. A 401 means the token is expired or missing. Retrying without refreshing the token is pointless. Retry only transient errors such as 502, 503, and network timeouts.

The problematic API wraps every HttpClient call in a try-catch that retries on any exception. There is no limit on retry count, no backoff delay, and no distinction between error types. The loop runs until the request succeeds or the thread is aborted, which can be minutes or hours.

data.text: The correct implementation uses a retry policy with explicit rules: which exceptions to retry, a maximum retry count, exponential backoff with jitter, and a circuit breaker that opens after too many failures. Polly is the standard library for this in .NET, and it integrates cleanly with HttpClient and ASP.NET Core.

cards.title: Infinite retry
cards.description: Retry forever on every exception with a fixed delay.

cards.title: Fixed count with fixed delay
cards.description: Retry a few times with the same delay between attempts.
cons: Thundering herd if all clients retry at the same time

cards.title: Exponential backoff with jitter
cards.description: Increase delay exponentially and add randomness.
cons: Longer total time before giving up

cards.title: Circuit breaker with fallback
cards.description: Stop retrying after repeated failures and return a cached or default response.

data.title: Which errors should be retried
items: 5xx Server Error: retry with backoff; the server may recover
408 Request Timeout: retry once; the network may have been momentarily slow
429 Too Many Requests: retry after the Retry-After header
Network timeout or connection reset: retry with backoff
400 Bad Request: do not retry; the request is malformed
401 Unauthorized: do not retry; refresh the token or return the error
403 Forbidden: do not retry; the user lacks permission
404 Not Found: do not retry; the resource does not exist

data.title: Use a library
data.text: Writing retry logic by hand is error-prone. Use Polly for .NET or the built-in resilience handlers in .NET 8+. They handle edge cases such as cancellation tokens, context propagation, and logging that hand-rolled loops miss.

items.question: Should I retry POST requests?
items.answer: Only if the API is idempotent or provides an idempotency key. Retrying a non-idempotent POST can create duplicate resources. Use idempotency keys for payment and order creation endpoints.

items.question: What is a safe maximum retry count?
items.answer: Three to five retries with exponential backoff is standard. More retries increase latency for the user and load on the downstream without significantly improving success rates.

items.question: How does HttpClientFactory help?
items.answer: HttpClientFactory manages socket exhaustion and integrates with Polly through AddTransientHttpErrorPolicy. Use it instead of creating HttpClient instances manually.

items.question: What if the circuit breaker opens during a critical operation?
items.answer: Return a fallback response: a cached value, a degraded mode, or a user-friendly error message. The circuit breaker protects the downstream at the cost of reduced functionality temporarily.

data.title: Implement bounded retries
data.description: Refactor an API client that retries every exception indefinitely into one with a bounded retry policy and circuit breaker.
steps: Identify all catch blocks that retry without conditions
Add Polly policies: retry only transient errors with a max of three attempts
Add exponential backoff with jitter between retries
Add a circuit breaker that opens after five consecutive failures
Log each retry attempt with the attempt number and reason
Write a test that mocks a 500 error and asserts the client retries three times then fails
data.expectedOutcome: The client retries transient errors with backoff, stops after three attempts, and opens the circuit breaker after five consecutive failures. Non-retryable errors fail immediately.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Retry only transient errors; never retry 4xx client errors
Use exponential backoff with jitter to avoid thundering herds
Bound retries with a maximum count and a circuit breaker
Use Polly or built-in resilience handlers instead of hand-rolled loops
data.takeaway: An unbounded retry is not resilience; it is an attack on your own infrastructure.
